name: Design a Mobile Release and Rollout System
intent: Ship an app through the stores so that a bad release is stopped within days, a bug in an installed version can still be switched off or fixed, and the backend keeps working for every version people still run.
prompt: Design the release and rollout system of a consumer app with 30 million monthly users on iOS and Android, shipped through the app stores. Unlike a web release, you cannot roll back an installed app, store review takes hours to days, users update over weeks, and some never update at all. A bad release must be stopped quickly, a bug found after release must be fixed for the people who already have the broken version, and the backend must keep working for six app versions at once. Design the path from build to store to users, and the server side that protects people on old and broken versions, not the app's features.
codeTitle: a staged store rollout, a crash gate, server flags and a minimum version on one 30-day model
finalIntro: One release, from a signed build to a halted rollout, a flag switched off and a hotfix.
functional: Build, sign and submit iOS and Android releases from a fixed release train
Roll a release out in stages and halt it automatically when its crash rate is worse than the old version's
Turn features on and off, and change configuration, without shipping a new build
Answer each request in the shape its app version understands, for the six versions in use
Move old versions forward with a soft nudge, a minimum supported version and a forced-upgrade screen
nonFunctional: A release whose crash rate is worse than the old version's is halted while fewer than 1% of active users have it
A bug behind a flag is switched off for users within 1 day of the decision, without store review
An API change never breaks a version that still has more than 1% of the active users
90% of the users on a broken build have the fix within 10 days of the decision, and a server-side mitigation is live within 1 hour
A forced upgrade locks out fewer than 1% of active users, and its threshold can be lowered in minutes without a new build

firstAttempt.text: A developer builds the release on a laptop, uploads it to both stores, and releases it to 100% of users the moment review passes. The app calls one API that is changed whenever the newest version needs it. If something breaks, the team ships another build and waits for review.
limits: A bad build reaches every user who updates, and nobody looks at crash numbers by version until reviews and support tickets pile up
A fix takes a store review of hours to days, and then users must install it, while the broken build stays on their phones
An API change made for the newest version breaks the older versions, which are still installed on millions of phones
New features ship switched on, so the only way to remove a bad one is another build
There is no way to tell how many users are on each version, or to move the ones on an unsupported version forward

nodes.label: Crash and error reports by version

steps.title: Build every release the same way, and make each request say which version it is
steps.problem: A build made on a laptop differs from one machine to the next, the iOS and Android builds drift apart, and nobody can say which commit a crashing build came from. The server also cannot tell a version 2 phone from a version 7 phone, so it cannot protect either one.
steps.fix: Run a release train: on a fixed schedule a branch is cut, built in CI from that exact commit, signed with keys held in a secrets store, and submitted to each store with a build number that maps back to the commit. Every API request carries the app version and platform in a header, and the server logs it, so the number of active users per version is known from the first day.
steps.tradeoff: A regular train makes releases small and routine, and a small release is easier to diagnose. A bug found on Monday waits for the next train unless a hotfix path exists, and the signing keys become something to guard and rotate.

steps.title: Release in stages, and watch crashes by version
steps.problem: Releasing to 100% when review passes sends a bad build to everyone who updates, and an installed app cannot be recalled. Crash numbers for the app as a whole mix all versions together, so a bad new version hides behind the healthy old ones.
steps.fix: Use the staged rollout the stores offer: 1% of eligible users first, then 5%, 20%, 50% and 100% on a timetable (Google Play releases to a percentage you choose, and Apple's phased release spreads an update over seven days). The app reports crashes, errors and slow starts tagged with its version and build number, and a dashboard shows the crash rate of each version next to the previous one. Reports are uploaded in batches when the network allows, so the numbers lag the truth by hours.
steps.tradeoff: A bug now reaches 1% of users first, and the harm depends on how fast someone notices. A full rollout takes about ten days, which is slower than a web deploy by design. Crash reports only come from phones that can send them.

steps.title: Let a gate halt the rollout, with a sample big enough to trust
steps.problem: A person who reads the dashboard each morning sees a bad build late: after a weekend, or once thousands of users have it. A gate that is too eager has the opposite problem: with a few hundred users on the new version, a handful of extra crashes looks like a spike and a healthy release is stopped.
steps.fix: A gate job compares the crash rate of the new version with the old version's for the same days. It waits until a minimum number of users have the new version, halts the staged rollout when the new rate is worse than the old one by more than a noise margin, and pages a person. A halt only stops new installs: people who already have the build keep it. A person then decides whether to resume, flip a flag or ship a fix.
steps.tradeoff: In the simulation a gate that samples 2,000 users stops a 3% crash after 72 users have hit it, instead of 6,424 when only support tickets notice. A sample of 200 reacts even sooner but halts healthy releases on noise; a sample of 20,000 almost never does, but it waits until the 20% stage.

steps.title: Ship features switched off, and control them with remote config
steps.problem: A halt does nothing for the people who already have the bad build, and a new build takes days to reach them. If a new feature is what breaks, shipping a new build to remove it is the slowest fix there is.
steps.fix: Put risky features behind flags that the app fetches from a config service when it starts, and caches. New code ships switched off, is turned on for a small share and then more, independently of the store percentage. The gate can flip the flag itself when the feature's own numbers go bad. A flag change reaches each phone the next time its app opens, not when its user next updates.
steps.tradeoff: A bug behind a flag is contained on day 2 in the simulation, against day 13 when it needs a new build. But a flag cannot remove a crash in code that has no flag, and the app must work on its baked-in defaults when it cannot reach the config service.

steps.title: Make the server adapt to the version, and keep a minimum version as a last resort
steps.problem: Six versions are in use. A change for the newest one breaks the older ones, which never fully go away because some users never update. Sooner or later an old version is insecure or too costly to support, but forcing it off locks out everyone who cannot update.
steps.fix: A version-aware gateway reads the version header and returns the shape that version understands: add fields, never remove or rename them, and translate for old clients. The adoption curve per version decides how long each shape must live. A minimum supported version in remote config works in two steps: a soft nudge first (a banner, a push), then a blocking screen with a store link for versions below it. The threshold is chosen from data on how many users sit below it and can update.
steps.tradeoff: Old apps keep working without a release, at the cost of an adapter layer that is maintained for months. In the simulation a minimum of the newest version on day 14 locks out 130,003 users, while a minimum of v5 locks out 23,401. A push nudge is best effort and does not reach everyone.

steps.title: Plan the hotfix path, and migrate the local database forward
steps.problem: Some bugs sit in code with no flag. The fix needs a new build, a store review of hours to days, and then users must install it. Meanwhile the app keeps its own data on the phone, which the new version changed, and a user may jump from version 4 straight to version 7.
steps.fix: Start with a server-side mitigation, such as no longer sending the data that triggers the crash to that version, and halt the rollout. Then fix on a branch from the released commit, ask for expedited review (both stores have a route for serious problems, with no guarantee), and release the hotfix to everyone at once with a nudge. Where the store rules allow it, an over-the-air update of an interpreted layer such as a JavaScript bundle can skip review, but native code cannot be changed that way. Local database changes are numbered migrations that run in order inside a transaction and are safe to run twice, so a phone that skipped a version applies every pending one, and each is tested from every supported old version.
steps.tradeoff: The first hours of a hotfix are decided by the server, not the store. The fix still only reaches users who install it, and a few percent never will. Testing migrations from every supported version multiplies with the support window, which is one more reason to keep that window short.

failures.scenario: The new build crashes for 3% of its users, and the crash is in code that has no flag
failures.impact: A server flag cannot help, and the broken build stays on every phone that installed it until its user updates.
failures.answer: The gate halts the staged rollout so no more users get the build, which keeps the number who hit the bug small. The team applies a server-side mitigation if one exists, fixes the bug on a branch from the released commit, asks for expedited review and releases the hotfix to everyone at once. Phones that updated in the meantime move to the fixed build over the following days. Next time, the risky code goes behind a flag.

failures.scenario: The gate watches only 200 users on the new version, and stops a healthy release over and over
failures.impact: A few random crashes look like a spike, the rollout is frozen for days at a small percentage, and most users stay on the old version for weeks.
failures.answer: The gate needs a minimum sample before it judges anything, a margin above the old version's rate that noise rarely crosses, and ideally the same finding on two checks in a row. A halt is a pause, not a rollback: a person looks at the numbers and resumes. A sample that is too large has its own cost, because the gate then waits for the 20% stage before it can act at all.

failures.scenario: The team raises the minimum supported version to the newest one, and 13% of users are locked out
failures.impact: Users with a phone too old to run the update, or with updates switched off, see a blocking screen they cannot get past, and they leave or flood support.
failures.answer: The minimum version is a last resort, chosen from data: how many users are below it, and how many of those can update. Announce it first with a soft nudge, raise it one version at a time, and keep the threshold in remote config so that a mistake can be lowered again in minutes without a build. A forced upgrade also needs the new build to be available to everyone, so it must not be raised while the store rollout is paused.

failures.scenario: A local database migration fails on some phones, and the app crashes at launch before it can fetch config
failures.impact: The kill switch lives in the config the app fetches at start-up, so the broken build can no longer be told to stop, and the user cannot even open the app.
failures.answer: Fetch config before anything risky, and add a crash-loop guard: after two crashes at launch the app starts in a safe mode, with the last known good config and without optional start-up work. Migrations are numbered, run in a transaction, are safe to run twice, and are tested from every supported old version, so skipping a version is fine. A failed migration leaves the old data in place, and the data can be rebuilt from the server when it is a cache of it.

alternatives.title: How to stop a bad release

options.name: Halt the store rollout and ship a fixed build
options.pro: Works for any bug, in any code
options.con: Takes days to reach users, and the broken build stays installed on the people who already have it

options.name: Switch the feature off with a server flag
options.pro: Reaches phones the next time they open the app, with no review
options.con: Only covers code that was put behind a flag before it shipped

options.name: Over-the-air update of the interpreted layer
options.pro: Can fix JavaScript-level bugs without a store review
options.con: Does not cover native code, depends on each store's rules, and adds a second release channel to test

alternatives.pick: Put every risky feature behind a flag, halt the store rollout automatically, and keep the hotfix path for what no flag covers. Use over-the-air updates only where the store rules clearly allow them.

alternatives.title: How long to support an old app version

options.name: Support every version forever
options.con: The adapter layer and the tests grow for ever, and old versions may carry known security holes

options.name: A fixed window, such as the last six versions
options.con: Ignores how many users are really on each version, so it can break a large group or keep a tiny one alive

options.name: A threshold from adoption data, then a nudge and a forced upgrade
options.pro: Retires a version when few users remain and warns them first
options.con: Needs the version header and the data, and some users still cannot update

alternatives.pick: Decide from the adoption data, nudge first, and force only when the share of users below the threshold who can update is known. Keep the threshold itself in remote config.

alternatives.title: What the rollout gate compares

options.name: A fixed crash-rate limit
options.pro: Easy to explain and to alert on
options.con: A normal bad week for the whole app, such as a platform update, trips it for a healthy release

options.name: The new version against the old one, on the same days
options.pro: Cancels what both versions share, so only the change shows
options.con: Needs a minimum sample and a noise margin, or small samples cause false halts

options.name: A person reading a dashboard
options.pro: Can weigh context that no rule knows
options.con: Slow at weekends and at night, and only as sharp as the last person who looked

alternatives.pick: Compare the new version with the old one on the same days, with a minimum sample and a margin, and let a person decide whether to resume a halted rollout.

roles.label: Phones
roles.description: The installed apps, from the newest version down to ones that are years old.

roles.label: Stores and gateway
roles.description: The app stores that review and stage releases, and the version-aware gateway in front of the API.

roles.label: Build and control
roles.description: The release train and build pipeline, the hotfix lane, the rollout gate and the API servers.

roles.label: Telemetry
roles.description: Crash and error reports from phones, grouped by app version.

roles.label: Config and device data
roles.description: Remote config and flags on the server, and the database on the phone.

quiz.question: A release has a bad feature behind a server flag and, separately, a crash in code with no flag. Both are already on many phones. What can be stopped without a new build?
options: Both, because halting the staged rollout removes the build from phones.
Only the flagged feature: the app reads its flag at start-up.
Neither, because every change to an installed app needs a store review.
Only the crash, because crash reports can be switched off on the server.
quiz.explanation: A halt stops new installs but cannot take the build off phones that already have it. A flag is read from the server when the app starts, so a flagged feature can be switched off with no review. A crash in unflagged code needs a fixed build, and turning off crash reports only hides it.

quiz.question: A rollout gate compares the new version's crash rate with the old one's, using only 200 users on the new version, and halts healthy releases every few days. What is the best fix?
options: Use a bigger sample and a wider margin over the old version's rate.
Lower the margin, so the gate halts as early as possible whenever anything looks wrong.
Remove the gate and rely on store reviews and support tickets to notice real problems.
Compare with the new version's own numbers from yesterday instead of the old version.
quiz.explanation: With a few hundred users, a handful of random crashes is enough to cross a small margin, so false halts are a statistics problem. A bigger sample and a wider margin fix that. A lower margin makes it worse, tickets arrive far too late, and comparing with yesterday ignores what both versions share.

quiz.question: A team raises the minimum supported version to the newest release and the support queue fills with locked-out users. What was the most likely mistake?
options: The blocking screen should have appeared on Android only, not on iOS.
The server should have deleted the accounts of everyone on an old version.
A minimum version works only if the app store hosts the threshold itself.
It locked out users who cannot or will not update.
quiz.explanation: Some users have phones too old for the update or have switched updates off, and a forced upgrade blocks all of them. The threshold should come from data, follow a soft nudge, and live in remote config so it can be lowered quickly. Platform and account deletion have nothing to do with it, and the threshold is served by your own config.
